title: How to Take Shilajit: Dosage, Methods & Absorption
description: How to take shilajit the right way: daily dosage in mg, dissolving resin without ruining fulvic acid, empty stomach vs food, and safety notes worth knowing.
bodyHtml:
Once you have a jar of resin in front of you, the next question is a practical one: how to take shilajit so it actually works and fits into your day. The answer is less complicated than the internet makes it sound. You need a sensible amount, a way of getting it into liquid without wrecking the delicate compounds inside, and enough consistency that your body has something to work with.

This guide covers dosage, the different formats, and the small details that affect absorption. If you are still wondering when to take it, we have a separate piece on the best time to take shilajit — this one is about how much and how.

How much shilajit per day?

The most common serving for purified shilajit resin is a pea-sized amount, roughly 300 to 500 mg, once daily. That is a genuinely small piece — smaller than most people expect the first time they open a jar. Human trials on purified shilajit have typically used doses in the 200 to 500 mg per day range, often split into two smaller servings, and that range is where the everyday wellness use sits.

If you are new to it, there is a good case for starting lower. Take around 150 to 250 mg daily for the first week or two, notice how you feel, and then move up to a full pea-sized serving if you are comfortable. Starting small is not about caution theatre; it simply gives you a clearer read on how your own body responds before you change anything else.

Going higher is not better. Doses above roughly 500 to 600 mg a day have not been shown to add anything for general wellness use, and very high intakes have not been well studied in controlled settings. Shilajit is a mineral-dense substance, not a protein powder — the useful dose is measured in milligrams, and more of it is simply more of it.

Capsules, sticks and tablets

If weighing out resin by eye is not your thing, standardised formats take the guesswork away entirely. Our Shilajit+ capsules and tablets give you a fixed amount per serving, and the honey sticks pre-portion it into a single-serve sachet. The trade-off is a little less flexibility in adjusting your dose. The resin lets you dial it in; the capsules let you stop thinking about it. Neither is wrong.

How to take shilajit resin, step by step

Resin is the traditional format and the one most people picture. Here is the method that works:

  • Scoop a pea-sized piece. Use the spoon that comes with the jar, or a clean utensil. Resin is sticky at room temperature and firmer when cold, so if it is stubborn, let the jar sit out for a few minutes or warm the spoon slightly.
  • Drop it into warm liquid. Around 60 to 70°C — comfortably hot, the temperature you would drink tea at, not boiling. Water, milk, or a non-caffeinated herbal tea all work.
  • Stir until fully dissolved. This usually takes 30 to 60 seconds. Properly purified resin dissolves cleanly and turns the liquid a dark amber-brown. Gritty residue or bits that refuse to dissolve are a red flag for quality.
  • Drink it reasonably soon. There is no need to rush, but there is also no benefit to letting it sit for an hour.

The temperature detail matters more than it might seem. Fulvic acid and several of the other compounds in shilajit are heat-sensitive, and boiling liquid can degrade them. So no adding it to a fresh cup of coffee straight off the boil, and no melting it in a pan. Warm, not hot.

Does shilajit absorb better on an empty stomach?

Taking shilajit on an empty stomach — say 30 to 60 minutes before your first meal — is the most commonly recommended approach, on the reasoning that nothing else is competing for absorption. It is a sensible default if your morning allows for it.

That said, the evidence here is more traditional than clinical, and it is worth being honest about that. If taking it with breakfast is the only version of the habit that survives a busy week, take it with breakfast. Consistency does considerably more for you than optimising the gap before your porridge.

A few things that genuinely do influence how you experience it:

  • Liquid choice. Water absorbs quickly and keeps things simple. Milk adds fats and protein, which some people find sits better and tastes far less bitter.
  • Taking it daily. Shilajit is not an acute-effect substance. Most people who notice anything describe it building over two to six weeks of consistent use, not overnight.
  • Purity of the product. Poorly processed shilajit does not just underperform — it can carry heavy metals like lead, arsenic and cadmium from the raw material. No dosing strategy compensates for that.

Safety and who should be careful

Purified shilajit is generally well tolerated at typical servings, but it is not for everyone. Reported side effects include allergic reactions, dizziness and changes in blood pressure. Raw, unprocessed shilajit should never be taken directly — the purification step exists precisely to remove contaminants.

If you are pregnant or breastfeeding, have haemochromatosis or another iron-overload condition, take blood pressure or blood thinning medication, or manage an ongoing health condition, speak to your doctor before starting. That is not a formality; shilajit contains iron and trace minerals in meaningful amounts, and interactions are plausible.

Building a routine you will keep

The best shilajit routine is the boring one. Pick a format that suits how you live, attach it to something you already do without thinking — the kettle going on, brushing your teeth — and give it a couple of months before drawing conclusions. Keep the jar somewhere you will see it. Do not try to make it a ceremony.
